prompt: A per-CPU scheduler runqueue uses a red-black tree keyed by soft deadline. Task A has soft deadline 120ms, B has 95ms, C has 110ms. All three are runnable. Which task does pick_next_task return?
choices: Task A, because it was enqueued first
Task B, because it has the lowest key
Task C, because it is the median value
Whichever task last called task_tick

prompt: A maintainer rejects folding a new best-effort, non-admission-controlled policy into the existing SCHED_DEADLINE class. What is the structural reason this would actually break?
choices: It would require a new syscall
It would make checkpatch.pl fail on style
It would corrupt the bandwidth-accounting invariant that assumes every task in that class is admission-controlled
It would exceed the maximum number of scheduling classes the kernel allows

prompt: In the RFC-review process, what does it mean when a maintainer replies to an RFC with zero comments on code style or variable naming?
choices: The code is approved for merge as-is
Style is not yet the bottleneck -- the design's shape hasn't been settled, so line-level review is premature
The maintainer did not read the patch
RFC patches are exempt from checkpatch.pl forever

prompt: You embed a new 40-byte struct sched_blbe_entity directly inside task_struct, unconditionally. On a system running 50,000 threads, how much additional kernel memory does this cost, and what review note from this lesson addresses it?
choices: 0 bytes, since task_struct is reference counted; no note needed
About 2,000,000 bytes (~1.9 MiB); flagged in the RFC's Interface/ABI section as a candidate for a Kconfig gate
About 2,000 bytes total, since the struct is shared across threads
40 bytes total, since only one instance exists per CPU

prompt: What does passing --rfc to git format-patch actually change?
choices: It compiles the patch against a test kernel before sending
It marks the patch so get_maintainer.pl skips it
It prefixes the email subject with RFC so reviewers know it is a request for comments, not a final submission for merge
It automatically CCs every subsystem maintainer

prompt: A new scheduling policy constant is being added for sched_setattr()/sched_getattr(). Why must it be appended after the existing SCHED_* values rather than inserted in logical order among them?
choices: Enum insertion order affects performance
Existing compiled userspace binaries depend on the numeric value of existing policy constants; renumbering breaks their ABI
The kernel build system requires policy values to be added in alphabetical order
sched_setattr() ignores the numeric value entirely

prompt: A maintainer objects to a new in-tree sched_class on the grounds that sched_ext (a loadable BPF scheduler mechanism) already covers this use case. Which revision actually answers that objection, rather than just resubmitting the same code?
choices: Rewriting pick_next_task to be more efficient
Adding more inline comments to the existing functions
Gating the feature behind a default-off Kconfig option and adding a documented rationale for why BPF-based scheduling isn't available on the target (e.g. CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL=n) embedded systems
Renaming the scheduling class to avoid confusion with sched_ext

prompt: In a kernel RFC cover letter, what is the specific purpose of the "Alternatives considered and rejected" section?
choices: To list every possible future extension of the feature
To preemptively address the obvious 'why not just use existing mechanism X' responses, so reviewers don't have to redo that design analysis for you in public
To satisfy a formatting requirement with no technical content
To list which other operating systems implement similar features
